reason: Right's charts keep readable labels at phone width and show a clean axis, while left's phone charts shrink their labels and values to tiny text.
Left's daily bar chart has colliding value labels against the average line on desktop and is cut to eight days on phone, while right's line and bar charts stay clean and legible on both.
Left's heat-shaded table stays compact on phone and reads at a glance, whereas right's phone table becomes a long stack of repeated cards, though left's phone bar chart drops the Dunmore label.
Right is clean and readable on both widths, while left's phone stacked-bar chart has tiny text and its per-statement tables stack into a very long repetitive column.
Left's phone layout is more compact with readable cards and a legible chart, while right's phone table stacks into a long list of cards, though right has a nice line chart on desktop.
Left has the stronger press-release hierarchy with kicker, italic deck, a labeled fact card and a contact card, and it holds up well in dark mode on the phone.
Right's stat cards, numbered claim steps and tighter sections look more finished than left's oversized empty list box.
Left has a more refined essay layout with a larger lead paragraph, serif subheads and a numbered closing list, and it reads comfortably on phone.
Right's single bill table with a highlighted total is compact and clear on both widths, while left's phone version has a tiny-label bar and long stacked tier cards.
Right adds a highlighted when/where callout, a timeline schedule and a warm sign-off, which gives clearer hierarchy and more polish than left's plain list.
